title.value: Production-Scale Impacts of Compaction Bands in Sandstone

note.value:
Thin, tabular, low-porosity and low-permeability compaction bands form extensive 3-D arrays throughout the upper 700 m of the eolian Aztec Sandstone in southeastern Nevada. Order-of-magnitude fluid-flow effects have previously been documented at the outcrop scale, but the potential for band arrays to influence flow at production scales remained an open question. Taking advantage of the stunning exposures of Aztec in the Valley of Fire State Park, we have produced a compaction-band map covering some 35 acres of nearly continuous outcrop, making it possible to simulate pressure communication and flow between wells at scales relevant to reservoir production, as well as to aquifer management and contaminant recovery.

The aerial photo-interpreted map reveals a prevailing sub-parallel to anastamosing band pattern with a dominant northerly trend, individual trace lengths ranging from tens to hundreds of meters, and an average inter-band spacing of about 1.5 m. Simulations were conducted on the raw map, with no attempt made to interpolate band patterns through areas of poor exposure or extrapolate them for increased coverage. Field checking indicated that average band spacing for the dominant pattern is more nearly 0.5 m, and that abundant subsidiary sets of generally thinner, lower angle deformation bands typically were not apparent in the aerial photo.

Nonetheless, 2-D simulations indicate that the bands as mapped would induce three to four-fold increases in driving pressure between injector-producer well pairs separated by as much as 200 m, when compared to the assumption of homogeneous, isotropic permeability. The bands also induce driving- pressure anisotropy, with pressure across the dominant trend exceeding pressure along it by as much as 30% for wells spaced 75 to 100 m apart. Anisotropy is even more pronounced for transport simulations. For a five- spot scenario with central injector, favorable alignment to the dominant band trend can increase oil recovery by a third over less favorable production configurations.

These significant effects could largely be captured assuming a homogeneous permeability anisotropy with kmax oriented parallel to the dominant band trend. Thus, armed with only spatially limited data on the orientation, volume fraction and relative permeability of compaction bands in a subsurface reservoir, production could be managed to mitigate and perhaps even capitalize on their impact.
Sternlof, Kurt and Karimi-Fard, Mohammed. (2005). Production-Scale Impacts of Compaction Bands in Sandstone. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: http://purl.stanford.edu/zw825wv2911
